input.description: Read the specification's where-clause section

content.content:
\section{Where Clauses}
\seclabel{where-clauses}

\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
\end{Grammar}


Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
in a \KWD{where} clause.
A \KWD{where} clause begins with
\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
and separated by commas.


A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
static variables that are not also static parameters.
The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.


A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
\begin{itemize}
\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
\item an arithmetic constraint,
\item a boolean constraint,
\item a unit equality constraint,
\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
\end{itemize}
A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
\KWD{where} clauses.

A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument
in an \KWD{extends} clause.
Such an occurrence would make the declared trait or object a subtype of
one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
which instantiation exclusion forbids
(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
the second of the three declarations below shows why.
\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
allowed, each with the way to write it.}

In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
it is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
Static parameters are invariant:
\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
%trait C[\S\]
%  getter item(): S
%end
%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
\end{Fortress}
so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a
\EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Animal}\rrbracket} with the same item.
The library's covariant collections are written this way.
\revision{revival-covariance}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves,
and gave the declaration above as the way to express covariance.
The type group's later design declares variance instead with a
\KWD{covariant} modifier on a static parameter
(the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012),
which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path;
the revival's decision record and row~404 of its gap ledger
say what is known of it.}


Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
to have a \KWD{where} clause. But the following trait
declaration is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C extends D[\T\]
%  where {T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{extends} D\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} would be a subtrait of \emph{every}
instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} would have all
of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. If trait
\VAR{C} inherits a method declaration that refers to \VAR{T}, it really
contains infinitely many methods (one for each instantiation of \VAR{T}).
However, instantiations of the \KWD{where}-clause variables are not
explicit from the program text as static parameters are.
It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site.
%%So every method invocation is annotated with static types by type inference.
If there is not enough information to infer which method is called,
type checking rejects the
program and requires more type information from the programmer.
Programmers always can provide more type information by using type
ascription as described in \secref{type-ascription}.
But trait \VAR{C} would also be a subtype of every pair of
different instantiations of \VAR{D},
which exclude each other by instantiation exclusion,
so no such restriction makes the declaration sensible:
that is why it is not allowed.
\revision{revival-every}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that this
declaration is legal. The paragraph above, the team's own account of why
such a trait is dangerous, is kept as the reason for the restriction stated
at the start of this section.}


Object or functional declarations may include \KWD{where} clauses,
under the same restriction.
The following declaration of an \TYP{Empty} list is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}
%  first() = throw Error
%  rest() = throw Error
%  cons(x) = Cons(x,self)
%  append(xs) = xs
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Empty} \KWD{extends} \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{first}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
\(  \VAR{rest}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
\(  \VAR{cons}(x) = \TYP{Cons}(x,\KWD{self})\)\\
\(  \VAR{append}(\VAR{xs}) = \VAR{xs}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \TYP{Cons} is declared in \secref{object-decls}.
Instead, the empty list is one object for each element type,
and each use writes the element type,
as in \EXP{\TYP{Empty}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}:
%object Empty[\T\] extends List[\T\]
%  first(): T = throw NotFound
%  rest(): List[\T\] = throw NotFound
%  cons(x: T): List[\T\] = Cons[\T\](x, self)
%  append(xs: List[\T\]): List[\T\] = xs
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Empty}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{first}()\COLON T = \;\KWD{throw}\:\TYP{NotFound}\)\\
\(  \VAR{rest}()\COLON \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \;\KWD{throw}\:\TYP{NotFound}\)\\
\(  \VAR{cons}(x\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{Cons}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x, \KWD{self})\)\\
\(  \VAR{append}(\VAR{xs}\COLON \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)\COLON \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \VAR{xs}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The library declares its empty collections and its empty optional value
(\secref{convenience-types}) the same way.
\revision{revival-empty}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave the
declaration marked ``Not allowed'' as its example of a \KWD{where} clause on
an object. It makes \TYP{Empty} a \EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for
every \VAR{T} at once, which instantiation exclusion forbids.
The declaration after it is the library's own shape; it needs the element
type written at each use until the static arguments of a generic object can
be inferred.}

----
    getter reverse(): Reduction[\()\] = VoidReduction

(** The identity of + and of juxtaposition for the number type named by the
    static argument alone, with no element in hand: the typecase over a
    %() -> T% witness, the witness of its result type, as %array1% takes
    one of its own.  Each type is tested before its supertypes. **)
additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 0
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(0))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(0))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(0)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(0))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(0, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(0.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 0.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => 0
    end

multiplicativeIdentity[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 1
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(1))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(1))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(1)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(1))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(1, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(1.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 1.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => 1
    end

object SumProdReductionPair[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\] extends ReductionPair[\T,T\]
    getter outer() = SumReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = ProdReduction[\T\]
end

object MaxSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }\]
        extends ReductionPair[\T,Maybe[\T\]\]
    getter outer() = MaxReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = LiftedCommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\](SumReduction[\T\])
end

object MinSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMin[\T\] }\]
        extends ReductionPair[\T,Maybe[\T\]\]
    getter outer() = MinReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = LiftedCommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\](SumReduction[\T\])
end

object SumReduction[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends CommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\]

    MaxSumReductionPair[\T\]
    distribute(r: MinReduction[\T\]): PossibleReductionPair[\Maybe[\T\]\] =

end

content.content:
A top-level function definition has a parameter list containing names of parameters and their types, and also a return type and a body expression.
A top-level abstract function declaration is similar, but has no body expression.
Top-level function declarations may be overloaded; that is, more than one function declaration may have the same name $f$.

Method definitions appearing in trait or object declarations are similar in form to function definitions; however, the keyword $\kwd{self}$
may be used within its body expression to refer to a value (the \emph{target object}) for which the method was invoked.
An abstract method declaration is similar, but has no body expression.
Method declarations may be overloaded; that is, more than one method declaration may have the same name $m$.

\input{fig-wellformeddecls}

\input{fig-covered}

Traits, objects, functions, and methods all have a (possibly empty) list of \emph{static type parameters}.
Associated with each static type parameter is (possibly empty) set of \emph{upper bounds}; any type used to instantiate the
type parameter must be a subtype of each of the declared upper bounds.
Each static type parameter of a method also has a (possibly empty) set of \emph{lower bounds}; any type used to instantiate the
type parameter must be a supertype of each of the declared lower bounds.
Each static type parameter of a trait has an associated \emph{variance}, which indicates ways in which different
instances of the same trait may extend or exclude each other.

Most of the forms of expression are fairly conventional.  The function creation expression
might be called a ````typed lambda expression'' in other languages.  We use the symbol $\apply$ to
distinguish application of function-typed values from invocation of (possibly overloaded) top-level functions.
Function invocations and method invocations each come in two forms, depending on whether static type arguments
are provided explicitly or are to be inferred.  The \emph{match expression} is a kind of compromise between
a conventional $\kwd{if}$ expression and a conventional $\kwd{typecase}$ expression.  One can get the effect
of $\kwd{if}\;e_1\;\kwd{then}\;e_2\;\kwd{else}\;e_3$ by declaring objects $\mathrm{True}\ob{\verythinmathspace}$ and $\mathrm{False}\ob{\verythinmathspace}$,
using them as values of predicates, and then writing
$e_1\;\kwd{match}\;x'\COLON \mathrm{True}\ob{\verythinmathspace} \Rightarrow e_2 \;\kwd{else}\;e_3$.

The type $\Any$ is a supertype of all types. The type $\Object$ is a supertype of every constructed type, that is, every trait type and every object type.
(The {\sc bnf} nonterminal $\Id$ is not used in the grammar, but is used in later figures.)
\section{Variations}

The algorithm just described works with covariant and invariant generic types, union types, and a set of constraints allowed on generic type parameters.  We can relax some of these restrictions and accept more varied inputs.

% \subsection{Additional constraints}
% Odersky~\cite{OderskyXXX} has noted that covariant data structures benefit from the ability to express type lower bounds.
% Covariant, widening list-append is one example of an operation that benefits from this.  Without the ability to declare that the parameter $U$ is a supertype of $T$, there is no type-correct way to express this.
% {\slantverbatim
% \begin{verbatim}
% trait List[\ covariant T \]
%    append[\ U dominates T \](x:U) : List[\ U \]
% end
% \end{verbatim}
% }
% In this use of a lower bound (on $U$), $T$ is effectively a constant because it is a parameter of the enclosing generic trait \textit{List} and not a parameter of the \textit{append} method.  This use of ````dominates'' does not present a problem for the algorithm.

trait LexicographicOrder[\T extends LexicographicOrder[\T,E\],E\]
        extends { StandardTotalOrder[\T\], ZeroIndexed[\E\] }

3:# Tuple comparisons and `LexicographicOrder`: the judgement
7:- **The question.** The library's `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` on pairs and triples, and `LexicographicOrder`'s `CMP`, compare elements whose type parameter has no bound. The compiled checker finds no `CMP` on an unbounded parameter: 18 sites (the ways note, section 1), and 8 more clauses it has not read yet behind the `typecase`s.
10:  - Lists, at the `where`-clause line: way 3, conditional extension, `List[\E\]` ordered exactly when `E` is, the team's own unbuilt feature, which PLAN's `where`-clause line already names as "item 43's first way". Its one site stays until then.
36:- *1c, the same bound on `LexicographicOrder`'s element*, forces `List[\E\]` to bound its `E` (`Library/List.fsi:67`), so lists of tuples, functions and `()` could not be written. That contradicts "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`" ("the library's generic containers are instantiated at tuples") and stops the pins at `ProjectFortress/tests/ResultBoundsRungB.fss:48-59`. Not taken.
40:**Way 3, conditional extension.** `List[\E\] extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`: a list is ordered exactly when its elements are. It is the only way that gives the specification's sentence its meaning, "lexicographic order when used to compare lists whose elements support these same comparison operators" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:294-295`), and the advanced library's "partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total" (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:520-523`). The grammar has it (`concrete-syntax.tex:465`), the team's test parses it (`ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss`), the front matter lists it as unsupported (`Specification/fortress/preamble.tex:95`), and the 2012 wind-down post wished it had been explored (the ways note, way 3). Every typed peer states the list order this way (Haskell's instance context, Rust's conditional impl, Scala's implicit `Ordering`; section 3, step 6). It is a checker, walk and code-generator change, and POSITIONS already gates `where` clauses that bind in an extends clause ("`Maybe`'s empty case"), with PLAN's `where`-clause line naming "item 43's first way" beside rows 433, 636 and 436 (`coordinator/PLAN.md:112`). **Taken for lists, at that line.** One point its rung must carry, by reading: `LexicographicOrder`'s `=` (`.fss:1936-1938`) is the only `=` a list has; under conditional extension a list of pairs would lose it and fall to `SEQV`, and `NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss:48`, which compares lists of pairs by `=`, would fail. So that rung keeps a structural `=` on `List` outside the condition.
42:**Way 4, conditional members.** A method's `where` clause on its trait's parameter leaves `LexicographicOrder` extending `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]` unconditionally, so a list of functions would claim an order and lack its operation (the ways note, way 4). Against "fast code a JVM can specialise", it dispatches per element at run time over arms with F-bounded parameters. Its private form, 6b, needs the compiled dispatcher to choose among two generic arms of different bounds, the shape on which the compiled run dies today (row 537, "Unable to read serialized data", gated for phase 5). And for lists it either loses lists of floats (a total arm beside `Any`) or answers `Comparison` where `LexicographicOrder` must answer `TotalComparison`. It keeps every pin, which is its only strength. Not taken.
48:**Way 7, monomorphic comparisons**, is combinatorial and loses every unwritten combination. **Way 8, an explicit comparator**, has no precedent among the library's operators and loses the operators themselves. **Way 9, drop them**, discards the team's 2007 declarations where its 2008 comment asks for bounds. **Way 10, a checker that defers or re-checks per instance**, revises "If there is no such declaration, then the call is undefined, which is a static error" (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:305-306`) and the checker's modular check, for 18 sites. **Way 11, leave them**, leaves 17 sites that the library's own device clears today. 73:- **Pavol's principle of 2026-09-22.** Where hardware behaviour can be written in bytecode, it gets its own spelling in the family the specification already has, as in Swift and Rust (`POSITIONS.md:52`). ∔ is that spelling for a bare `iadd`.

One sentence at each of three internal-appendix passages.
115:One sentence goes further than the rule. `trait-parameters.tex:339-340`: "A where-clause variable may not appear as a static argument in an extends clause."
117:- A variable pinned down by a constraint on the declaration's own parameter is a different case. Take `trait Foo[\S\] extends Bar[\T\] where {S extends Baz[\T\]}`. Under instantiation exclusion, a given `S` extends at most one `Baz` instantiation, so each `S` yields exactly one `Bar` instantiation. By reading, the rule allows this, and the sentence refuses it.
120:- Nothing on microGPT's path uses a where clause: there is none in `explorations/run-c4/src/` or `explorations/apl/mg/`, and the code generator refuses any where clause on an object (`CodeGen.java:4088`, judgement section 3.1).
132:S met one conflict inside the team's own record and stated it plainly. The library's comment at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:923-924` says `Nothing` "will become a non-parametric singleton when we get where clauses working". That comment is Maessen's of 2008 (`f861cca4d`), before the rule. The callout quotes it and says the rule closes that road (`convenience.tex:74-79`). That is the right weighing under `POSITIONS.md:58`.
142:- **The wind-down post.** It names "conditional inheritance via where clauses" among the three things the team wished it had explored (`design-intent-sources.md:57`). S's where-clause sentence does not touch that: a where clause that constrains the declaration's own parameters stays legal (decision record section 1, item 21).
143:- **What the sentence does close.** It closes the hidden-type-variable supertype. The design record has no argued source for that feature at all (`design-intent-sources.md:102`), and the where calculus is its only formal home (`Specification/appendices/calculi/where/calculus.tex:21-31`, now marked as predating the rule).
150:- **Row 331.** Pavol's decision on row 331 (2026-09-21) gated the bare `Nothing` on "where clauses binding a type variable in an extends clause" (`POSITIONS.md:49`). S's sentence forbids that gate outright. The judgement proposed re-gating it on static-argument inference, and that is parked (`PLAN.md:120`). The record knows this. It is one more reason the where-clause sentence should be narrowed or its breadth recorded as chosen.
153:- **What reached Pavol.** The calculi stop reached him and was answered (`POSITIONS.md:116`). The where-clause sentence's breadth did not, because no one saw it as a choice.
158:Every revised passage carries a decision of Pavol's or the team's later Types chapter, in the team's own form, with the original kept and route C recorded. The where-clause sentence is a defensible deviation inside the rung: it matches what both paths do, but it is broader than the rule and no one decided the breadth.
180:  - `IntLiteral` coerces into ℕ32 wherever one is needed, so every use the specification names still works. Defensible.
203:- **Types never erased.** Every generic instance is stamped out with its arguments in its name (`map/design-intent-sources.md:114`; `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation`). Design B puts a size into the slot a type argument already has, so a size is carried at run time exactly where a type is.
217:- **What Z found beyond its scope, and where it sits.** Z's skeptics and repair round found three compiled-path defects that types share with sizes and that predate Z:
241:Design B and the factory are Pavol's. Z built them from the team's own factory, `CONST` channel, dispatcher structures and reserved slots. Its deviations are argued and small. What is not in the spirit is where its findings went, not the code: three defects on the path of phases 4 to 6 stayed rows, and its list for Pavol stopped at the handover.
253:3. **A size's range was decided by a judge and not shown to him.** A size read as a value is exact at any magnitude, gated up to 2^64-1. The specification says a nat parameter appears where an ℕ32 variable can.

# The array questions: every way, the library's own first

## In short

- **Decision D, the model's sized types.** D1 sizes in the model's types through the library's own devices (the re-based diff); D2 the vocabulary over the unsized `Array`, the model unchanged; D3 D1 in the specification's `T^n` notation, which neither path takes today; D4 every size static from the top, the batch size fixed at compile time.

- **A size known only at run time.** 4a the library's `reflect`, with the checker taught the team's commented rule for opening it; 4b `reflect` built in over design B's size factory; 4c run-time sizes stay unsized; 4d no run-time sizes in the step; 4e a `typecase` that binds a size, after `where` clauses.
- **The element width.** 5a `RR64` as written; 5b `RR32` throughout, with float32 goldens from the reference; 5c the model generic in its width; 5d the width named once by a type alias; 5e `RR32` storage with `RR64` sums, the draft's `Extended`.
- **The bounds of `Vector` and `Matrix`.** 6a `T extends Number` as landed; 6b the storing objects take their traits' bound, a slip under every way; 6c the library's `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, alone or beside `Number` in the library's two-trait form; 6d a bound per operation, the products moved out of the traits; 6e the specification's algebra, after `where` clauses; 6f arithmetic on `Number`, against route A.
- **The re-based diff, measured today.** The model: 21 lines out, 29 in, the same lines as on 2026-09-27. C4's own errors on the compiled checker: 26 as written, 14 with the diff (24 and 12 on 2026-09-27; the three `fail` errors are gone and five numeral powers are newly refused as an ambiguous coercion). The diagnostic copies: 28 and 18 with the tuple bindings split; 14 with the dead sizes also deleted; 7 when the powers are written so one declaration applies, the old 10 less the three `fail` errors. Walk: 40 of 40, every value identical.
- **Measured here for the first time.** The library's selection device returns a store written for `RR64` alone through the library's `cast`, and it checks and runs on both paths, sized too; a plain factory beside the generic one compiles and dispatches, and walk refuses the pair. The storing objects' missing bound is a slip: fixed, 19 of V1's 36 errors go and none is new. The ring bound on `Vector` and `Matrix` clears all 36 and brings 8 new errors, because `MultiplicativeRing` is open where `Number` is closed; on the scalar-extension block walk refuses it. Written beside `Number` in the library's two-trait form, it clears 34 and brings 1, and the checker spends several times longer on the library's overloads. The storing objects made at run time with `primitiveArray` clear the 8 storage errors of item 15 with none new, and C4 runs unchanged. `RR32` and `RR64` kernels on the JVM show no difference beyond their noise.
- **The forks, in the order they need deciding** (section 8): item 15; the bounds; a run-time size; the element width; decision D; decision A.

## 0. Words used below

- A *size* is a `nat` static parameter: a number in a type, as in `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. A *sized* type carries one; an *unsized* type, `Array[\RR64, ZZ32\]`, does not.
- A *store* is the object that holds an array's elements. Today every store is `PrimitiveArray[\T, n\]`, a boxed Java array under walk (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:18-30`).
- *Boxing* is holding each number as its own heap object; on the compiled path an `RR64` is an `FRR64` object (FACTS § Execution model, line 12).
- *Stamping* is the class loader writing one class per instantiation of a generic from its template, by substituting names (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 0).
- A *witness* is an argument that carries a static argument and nothing else. The library has two: `__thrower[\T\]`, a function of type `() -> T` never called (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2372`), and `N[\n\]`, an object whose type carries a size (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`).
- *Opening* a size is binding a size parameter to a number known only at run time, inside the code that runs with it. The type theory calls it unpacking an existential.
- A *bound* is the `extends` clause of a type parameter: `T extends Number` admits only number types for `T`.
- *The distance stage* is the gate's full checker measurement of the one library (`coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`); its classes V1, V2 and Z1 are the array ones (`coordinator/tools/distance/classify.py:59-104`).

4. **The element width (question 5).** `RR64` or `RR32`? Ways: 5a `RR64` as written; 5b `RR32` throughout, with new float32 goldens from the reference and rung V first; 5c the model generic in its width; 5d the width named once by a type alias, after aliases are built; 5e `RR32` storage with `RR64` sums, the draft's `Extended`. Every type line of decision D's diff and every store of decision A follows from it.
5. **The model's sized types (decision D).** How do sizes enter the model's text? Ways: D1 the re-based diff, 21 model lines out and 29 in; D2 the vocabulary over the unsized `Array`, the model unchanged and its shapes unchecked; D3 D1 in the specification's `T^n` notation, which neither path takes today; D4 sizes static from the top, the batch size fixed at compile time. D1's 10 bridge lines are question 4's answer, and its 7 `rows(rmsn[\E\], …)` lines are the inference of a generic function passed as an argument, which the specification promises and its inference chapter does not yet describe.
6. **What puts `double[]` under the generic traits (decision A).** Ways: A1 the library's witness `typecase` with its `cast` (measured on both paths); A2 a plain factory beside the generic one (compiled yes, walk refuses the pair today); A3 a factory name per element type; A4 the loader stamps an `RR64` class, the team's `Unbox` direction; A5 a special type, as `ZZ32Vector`. None is faster alone; decision B (phase 6) unboxes the traffic.

Walk takes them. No ledger row names it; the declarations are `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:278` and `:358`.
- **The comment that decision D's note of 2026-09-27 called the library's own is the revival's.** "sized arrays under a compiler need per-shape declarations beside these" was written by the revival on 2026-09-23 (`c2b4e2c95`) and reworded on 2026-09-28 (`581356f32`); today it reads "a static checker sees only Array[\T,I\], so the rank and size of a sized argument are lost to it in the result" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2595-2600`). The team's own statement on per-type storage is Maessen's commit message of 2008 (section 3).

Readings of my own are marked "(my reading)". -->

# Array fork 2, judged: the bound of `Vector` and `Matrix`

## In short

- **The question.** `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` add, subtract and multiply values of `T` in their bodies, and the scalar-extension block adds, subtracts, `MIN`s and `MAX`es a `T` with each element of an `Array[\T,I\]`; `Number` declares `asFloat` and `=` and nothing else. Which bound on `T` gives those bodies their arithmetic? It holds 25 of the 153 errors the compiled checker reports on the one library: 15 arithmetic refusals at `(T, T)` or `T`, the 8 of the scalar block, and 2 "does not satisfy the bound" sites at the factories `vector` and `matrix` (section 1).
- **What the history says.** The team's bound did carry arithmetic. Their `Number` extended `AdditiveGroup[\Number\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\Number\]` and `StandardMinMax[\Number\]` and declared `+`, `-`, juxtaposition and `MIN` on any two numbers, every result an `RR64` (`git show 75cca6683:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, lines 273-313). Route A, his decision, took that arithmetic off `Number` and gave it to each sibling at its own type (POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A)"; `d846e3644`). The fork is the obligation route A left on the arrays (FACTS, "Route A's generic container obligations still need body-level checks"). The bound that says on the flat tower what the team's bound said on theirs is "a number that is a ring at its own type".
- **The library's own way.** Since answer 7 the library bounds generic arithmetic by its algebra trait at the element's type: `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]`, `PROD[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3284-3301`), and where one trait is not enough it writes two, `MaxSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }\]` (`:3262`, `:3268`). Its products are methods so that views override them: `TransposedMatrix` overrides `scale`, `rmul` and `lmul` (`:2800-2802`), and his diagonal overrides `mul` (POSITIONS, "The vocabulary's scalar drops and the diagonal").
- **The recommendation.** The library's two-trait bound, each declaration asking for what its body uses: `Vector`, `Matrix`, their storing objects, factories, norms and products take `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` (29 component lines, 32 api lines); the scalar block takes a bound per operator, `{ Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }` on `+` and `-`, `{ Number, StandardMin[\T\] }` on `MIN`, `{ Number, StandardMax[\T\] }` on `MAX` (8 and 8). `Number` stays, so its exclusions, its `asFloat` and the specification's "all elements of vectors and matrices must be numbers" stay; the algebra trait brings the arithmetic. No body, model or specification line changes. On the flat tower every number type is a ring at its own type, the integers included (`Integral[\I\] extends MultiplicativeRing[\I\]`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:443`), so no integer array is excluded. **Default: the same.**
- **Measured today** (section 3), on a copy of the library through the gate's distance stage and under walk: the type-check stage clears all 23 arithmetic and block sites and uncovers the one parent-trait error at `scale` (`:2399`), as read; the two factory sites stay, as read; walk's seven array tests print the same as on the unchanged copy. And one thing not read: the checker's overloading stage crashes on the api and the component, and the export stage with it, "ClassCastException: UnionType cannot be cast to BaseType" in the team's `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.boundsSubstitution` (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:474-477`, David Chase, 2012, "TODO: FIX THIS FOR OPS", unchanged since), because the checker reads the closed `Number` as the union of its members and the meet of two bounds then comes back a union. One call is refused for the same reason (the norm's `squaredNorm(me)`, `:2483`). So the way needs a checker fix first, and the 09-29 timing question is not answered: the Meet Rule check that was slow then did not run today.
- **A batch 13 rung, in two halves** (section 5): the checker's `boundsSubstitution` taught a bound list whose meet is a union, test first with an expected-failure compiled test; then the 77 library lines, the distance stage before and after by row and line. It clears 23 of the fork's 25 and uncovers 1: 153 to about 131.
- **What it leaves.** The 2 factory sites, a checker slip no bound cures (section 2.2); the bodies typed by the parent trait, 10 with `:2399`, which need their own list of ways; row 437's numeral `0` in `matrix(v)`, whose repair `v.zero` the bound now permits; a `Vector` of numerals (`IntLiteral` is a `Number` and not a ring), which nothing on record makes; walk's `Bottom` for a two-bound parameter that no call fixes (row 591), which the arrays' calls all fix; the code generator's erasure of a two-trait bound, unmeasured, which `MaxSumReductionPair` already carries to the switch-over.
- **What it bends.** The letter of "no blanket ring bound" on the two traits, not its reason (integer arrays), and the placement of the array questions after the switch-over, which PLAN's batch 13 line already brings forward for this fork (section 6).

## 0. Words used below

- A *bound* is the `extends` clause of a type parameter: `T extends Number` admits only number types for `T`. A bound with two traits, `T extends { A, B }`, admits only types that extend both.
- A *self-typed trait* is a trait whose parameter is the type that extends it: `RR64 extends MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\]`. The papers call it the self-type idiom (section 2.4).

# Array fork 3, a size known only at run time: the judgement

## In short

- **The question.** How a number computed when the program runs becomes a size that the compiled checker accepts and the compiled path runs. Today `reflect(x)` answers the trait `NatParam`, and the checker does not know that every `NatParam` is some `N[\n\]`, so it refuses the library's own run-time factories and subarrays: 10 sites of the 153 (section 1), 4 more hidden behind two checker crashes, and the model's three bridges later.
- **The judgement.** Way 4a: the team's own clause, `trait NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, written as a comment in 2007 and never built, uncommented; the checker taught the one rule it states: an argument of type `NatParam` passed where `N[\n\]` is expected opens `n` as that value's own size, for that call. It is the library's own device to the letter, the papers' existential subtyping rule applied to a size, the specification's own `where`-clause variable, and what the peers do (Haskell's `someNatVal`). Way 4b, `reflect` built in as a primitive, clears nothing more once item 15's rule accepts `reflect`'s body, and its run-time economy cannot be measured before the switch-over: deferred, not refused. Ways 4c, 4d and 4e each leave the library's own factories refused or wait on `where` constraints.
- **The default.** 4a as the team wrote it; 4b when a compiled measurement asks for it.
- **The cost.** One checker rung of item 15's size: three checker files, two library lines, about ten lines in walk's loader, two specification sentences and an Appendix I entry, tests first. The compiled half (a call whose size is read off the argument's descriptor, through the dispatcher's own closure-table device) waits for the switch-over, as item 15's loader half does.
- **The order.** Beside item 15's rung, in batch 13's gate. Its library line must not land before item 15's part (b), or the checker would hold that `NatParam` excludes `N[\0\]` (section 5).
- **What it bends.** One sentence the revival itself wrote on 2026-09-28 (a listed type may not name a `where`-clause variable) is widened by a clause; his "Sizes" entry is read anew (an opened size is bound, not unknown). Nothing of his is reversed.

## 0. Words

- A *size* is a `nat` static parameter: a number in a type, the `16` of `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. A *sized* type carries one; the *unsized* `Array[\E, ZZ32\]` does not.
- A *run-time size* is a size known only when the program runs: a file's length, the batch's rows, the parameter vector's length.
- A *witness* is an argument that carries a static argument and nothing else: `N[\n\]`, an object whose type carries a size (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi:27`), and `__thrower[\E\]`, a function never called (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2439`).
- `reflect(x)` turns a `ZZ32` into a witness: it answers the trait `NatParam`, whose every value is an `N[\n\]` (`NatReflect.fss:15-31`).
- *Opening* a size is binding a size name to a number known only at run time, inside the code that runs with it. The type theory calls the type "there is an `n` such that this is an `N[\n\]`" an *existential*, and opening it *unpacking*.
- A *skolem* is the fresh name the checker gives an opened size: equal to itself and to nothing else.
- A *`where`-clause variable* is a static variable that is not a static parameter, bound in a `where` clause (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:324-328`).
- *The distance* is the checker's error count on the one library; a *site* is one error's file and line (`compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`).

Row 664 records them. The brief's "9" is the count of `reviews/array-forks-now.md` before batch 12's rung R typed `r'.lower` and uncovered `:2257` (`reviews/batch-12-review.md:14`).

# The array judgements against POPL 2019

## In short

- **Point 1, fork 2's F-bound: stands, with a sentence.** The paper admits an F-bound on a trait's parameter and drops one on a method's (p. 11:10, p. 11:11). The bound lands on both kinds: 5 traits and objects in the admitted form, and 38 generic functions and operators (the api's count: 30 of the family, 8 of the block; 32 lines in the component) outside the paper's theorem, beside the 30 F-bounded functions the api already has (`SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MIN`, the tuple orders). Same ground: in every one, `T` stands at an invariant position of a parameter or of the result, so its bound is checked after substitution and never solved, which is all the paper's restriction protects. Nothing is shown unsound. Neither [Anc-Same-Trait] nor [D-Method] touches the bound.
- **Point 2, the block's per-operator bounds: stands, with a sentence.** The paper has no library, numbers or operators, so it says nothing on "no blanket ring bound". It sharpens one reason of the judgement: in the paper's own calculus two traits never exclude, so the block's mirror pairs, `(Array[\T,I\], T)` beside `(T, Array[\T,I\])`, are a valid overload set only through `Number`'s closure, the extension the paper leaves out (pp. 11:3, 11:25). `Number` in each bound is what the Meet Rule needs; the ring alone lost it.
- **Point 3, fork 3's opening: stands, with a sentence.** The paper's run-time rule gives a parameter at an invariant position the value's own argument (p. 11:19): the opened size at run time. Its static rule has ground argument types and existentials on domains only (p. 11:3), so it says nothing on reading `NatParam` as "some `N[\n\]`"; that warrant stays the 2011 paper's existential subtyping, which fork 3 cites. One line for phase 5: a call's static return type is carried to run time as a ground type (pp. 11:16-17), and a type holding an opened size is completed from the argument's descriptor first.
- **Point 4, what else: one row changes.** Row 682, `f(x: NatParam)` beside `f[\nat n\](x: N[\n\])`, "unsettled" on record: under the clause the two domains are equivalent, and the paper's No Duplicates rule refuses the pair (Theorem 4.1, p. 11:15); the checker's refusal is the paper's verdict, walk's acceptance at load is walk's looser check. Rows 686 and 690 (fork 2's follow-ups): the paper's static rules accept both programs, so the refusals are the checker's, as the rows say.
- **Point 5, batch 14: stands, with a sentence.** The self-typed rung's confinement of rule (a) to bodies is what keeps declared signatures within the paper's ground: matching's completeness assumes no type parameter inside an intersection in a declared type (pp. 11:21-22), and [Return-Test] compares domains (p. 11:13); the 18 false Return Type Rule errors of the unconfined probe were those two places. The rung should say so. Rule (b) and the self type itself are beyond the paper; [D-Method] adds nothing to invariant generics.
- **Nothing reverses.** Both recommendations stand; what rung N built on fork 3 and what batch 13b is landing on fork 2 stand; the pending answers on items 13 and 52 can be given at their defaults.

## 0. The paper, in the words needed

- **FGFV**, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with Variance": traits like Java interfaces, objects like final classes, trait type parameters with variance marks and upper bounds, method type parameters with lower and upper bounds, calls that write no static arguments (p. 11:8; extract lines 46-56).
- **Trait parameters' bounds** are checked under an environment binding the parameters themselves ([D-Trait], p. 11:10), so an F-bounded trait parameter is admitted by the rule's form (extract lines 283-285).
- **Method parameters' bounds** may not name a method type parameter: "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (p. 11:11; recheck line 20, quoting). The scope of a method type parameter extends to its right, and the run-time solve works right to left on that account (p. 11:11, p. 11:19; extract lines 196-207). The paper says restriction (1), the scoping, "makes dynamic dispatch more efficient" and restriction (2), the bounds, "makes it consistent" (recheck line 20, quoting).
- **[D-Method]** checks that a covariant or contravariant trait parameter appears only in positions of its variance; "type parameters of objects and invariant type parameters of traits are invariant" (pp. 11:11-12; extract lines 106-110).
- **[Anc-Same-Trait]**: a class extending two instances of one trait extends an instance below both; blanket for an invariant parameter (p. 11:11; extract lines 68-79).
- **The static rules**: a generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is existentially quantified over its type parameters" (p. 11:3); No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type over domains, specificity by subtyping of domains, "sound but not complete", narrowed by existential reduction, which collects the constraints that keep an intersected domain off `Bottom` (pp. 11:12-14; extract lines 136-160). Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration for every call; "No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric" (p. 11:15; extract lines 161-164).
- **The run time**: ilks; every call carries its static return type (pp. 11:16-17); [Dispatch] matches the ilks against the domain, matches the static return type against the declared one, and solves by "taking the intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed, never `Bottom` (pp. 11:17-19; extract lines 186-207). Completeness of matching "assumes that a matched type holds no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection", which every declared type meets (pp. 11:21-22; extract lines 256-260).
- **Left out**: functional methods, closed types, nominal exclusion, modularity, top-level functions (pp. 11:3, 11:25); self types, a numeric tower, coercion, `nat` parameters (extract lines 277-285; recheck line 21).

## 1. Fork 2's bound is an F-bound

**What carries it.** The half's commit `d3d31b5b2` writes the bound on two kinds of declaration:

- Traits and objects, 5 in the component and 2 in the api: `trait Vector[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\]`, `object __DefaultVector[\...\]`, `trait Matrix[\...\]`, `object __DefaultMatrix[\...\]`, `object TransposedMatrix[\...\](mem: Matrix[\T,s1,s0\])` (`git show d3d31b5b2 -- Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, the five `+trait` and `+object` lines).
- Generic functions and operators, 32 in the component and 38 in the api: the factories `vector`, `tabulatedVector`, `matrix`, the products `pmul`, `DOT` and `juxtaposition`, the sums and differences `+` and `-` on the family, `squaredNorm`, the norm `||v||` (24 and 30), and the block's `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX` (8 and 8).

**The trait-level bound is in the paper's admitted form.** [D-Trait] checks a trait parameter's bounds under the parameters themselves (p. 11:10), so `T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` on `Vector` is well formed by the rule's form, as the library's twelve F-bounded traits are (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:73`, `:175-229`, `:265`, `:277`, `:446`, `:1341`, `:1508`, `:1516` at `HEAD`). The `nat` parameter beside it is outside the paper altogether.

**The function-level bound is outside the paper's theorem.** Restriction (2) excludes a method type parameter from every upper bound (p. 11:11). Fortress's top-level functions and operators are the paper's receiver-free case (extract lines 405-408, by reading), so `pmul[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat k\]` and the block's `opr +[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\]` are Naden's rewrite shape, `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X`, which the extract notes the paper excludes (extract lines 348-349, 377-378). The api already holds 30 such declarations: `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX`, `BIG MINMAX`, the four `BIG MIN_MIN` kin, `BIG BITXOR` (`.fsi:1973-2075`) and rung O's tuple orders (`.fsi:2633-2643`). The half adds 38. So the fork roughly doubles what stands outside Theorem 5.11, and adds no new kind of declaration. FACTS already says the theorem does not cover the library's F-bounded functions (FACTS, "The team's latest word on types ..."; recheck § 1.4).

**Same ground.** The restriction exists for the solve: a right-to-left pass that takes the intersection of ground upper bounds (p. 11:19), which an upper bound naming the parameter would not give. Where the ilk fixes the parameter at an invariant position, lower and upper bound coincide and the declared bound is a ground check after substitution, never a type to solve for; the recheck read this for `Generator[\T\]` (§ 1.4, "the bound is checked and never solved"). Every declaration of the family fixes `T` so: by a parameter `Vector[\T,k\]`, `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` or `Array[\T,I\]` (invariant), or, for the nullary factories `vector[\T,s0\]()` and `matrix[\T,s0,s1\]()`, by the result `Vector[\T,s0\]`, which the paper's second step reads off the call's static return type (p. 11:18) and the compiled path off the written static arguments. `additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T` (`.fss:3230`) is already that result-only shape. The judgement's own line holds: "the arrays' calls all fix `T`" (`array-fork2-judgement.md:173`).

**Dispatch and instantiation at run time.** The class loader stamps `Vector[\RR64,16\]` from the static arguments; the paper's run time has every type parameter "instantiated with ground types" (p. 11:17); the two agree. The dispatcher scans overloads most to least specific by the ilks, [R-Method]'s shape (p. 11:17; extract lines 180-185). Where the paper's instance and the value's differ, a parameter nothing fixes (recheck § 1.6), no array call arrives. The dispatcher does not yet carry the call's static return type (`OverloadSet.java:2048`), a phase 5 line already on PLAN; the arrays add nothing to it.

**[Anc-Same-Trait] and [D-Method].** The ancestor rule bears on the bound's satisfiers and the family's extenders, not on the bound: each number type extends `MultiplicativeRing` at itself once (`Integral[\I\] extends MultiplicativeRing[\I\]`, `.fsi:446`; `RR64` and `QQ` likewise), `TransposedMatrix[\T,s0,s1\]` extends `Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]` once, C4's `Diag` extends `Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]` once. [D-Method] constrains variant parameters' positions; Fortress's generics are invariant, so it is met trivially, and a bound is not a method position in the paper (it is checked by [D-Trait]). FACTS already draws the one consequence, that no self-typed algebra trait can be covariant (recheck § 1.1).

## 7. Read against the full text

Written after the curator took option 2 and the paper was committed beside its extract (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.pdf`, its text `ParkPOPL2019.txt`). The pages below were read from the PDF (its pages 10 to 22 are the article's 11:10 to 11:22; the figures are images), and the line numbers are the text file's. Nothing above this section is changed; where the full text overturns a sentence above, this section says so.

### 7.1 The rules at the source, claim by claim

- **Figure 5, the No Duplicates Rule (p. 11:13).** Three rules, any one sufficient: [No-Dup-Triv] for different names, [No-Dup-Not-Less], `¬(Δ ⊢ dom(d) ⊑ dom(d'))`, and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr], `¬(Δ ⊢ dom(d') ⊑ dom(d))`. The prose: "if the domain type of one declaration is not a subtype of the domain type of the other, they satisfy the rule ([No-Dup-Not-Less] and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr])" (p. 11:12, lines 609-611). So two declarations are duplicates exactly when their domains are each below the other. *Confirms* § 4's caveat, and *overturns* the extract's compression, "neither domain is below the other" (`ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:150`), which should read "not each below the other"; the extract is not among this check's files, so that is reported, not repaired.
- **Theorem 4.1 (p. 11:15).** "We first show that the more specific relation of method declarations is a partial order. It is clearly reflexive and transitive since the existential subtype relation is reflexive and transitive. The No Duplicates Rule guarantees that it is antisymmetric" (lines 784-786). *Confirms* § 4: antisymmetry is what the rule buys, and it needs exactly that no two distinct declarations have equivalent domains.
- **[D-Trait] and [D-Object] (Figure 3, p. 11:10).** Both begin `Δ' = Δ ∪ {{} <: P <: {ξ}}`, `distinct(P)`, `Δ' ⊢ ξ ok`: a trait's or an object's parameter bounds are checked under the parameters themselves. *Confirms* § 1, and extends it to the three storing objects: [D-Object] admits `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` on `__DefaultVector`, `__DefaultMatrix` and `TransposedMatrix` as [D-Trait] does on `Vector` and `Matrix`.
- **[Binding-Step] (Figure 4, p. 11:11), restriction (2).** `FV(χ') ⊆ parameters(Δ) ∪ {P}` and `FV(η') ⊆ parameters(Δ)`: a method type parameter's lower bounds may name the parameters to its left, its upper bounds may name only the class's parameters; the prose, "(2) no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (lines 565-570). *Sharpens* § 1: `pmul[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat k\]` fails the figure's premise at `T ∈ FV(η')`, not only the prose; the 38 are outside the theorem as stated. The bound of a method's own parameter is checked here, under [D-Method]'s premise `Δ ⊢ [[{ξ} <: Q <: {ξ}]] ok`, so § 1's parenthesis "(it is checked by [D-Trait])" holds for a trait parameter's bound only; the point it serves, that a bound is no position of the method's arrow type, stands.
- **[D-Method] (Figure 3, p. 11:10; p. 11:12).** The variance premise is on the arrow type alone, `(V = =) ∨ (∀T. ((τ → ω) ≠ T[P]) ∨ (Δ ⊢ T variance V))`, and the type context's fourth clause, "type parameters of objects and invariant type parameters of traits are invariant" (lines 592-595). *Confirms* §§ 1 and 5: met trivially by invariant generics.
- **[Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11).** `T[[γ]] ∈ {J}`, `Δ ⊢ T[[γ]] <: T[[α]]`, `Δ ⊢ T[[γ]] <: T[[η]]`. *Confirms* §§ 1 and 4: each number type and each extender of the family at one instance.
- **The existential reading and [E-Sub] (§ 4.2, p. 11:12; Figure 6, p. 11:14).** `dom(d) = ∃[[K]](α)`; "an existential type ∃[[K]]α is a subtype of another existential type ∃[[K']]α' if there exists a substitution σ for the type parameters bound in K' that makes σα' a supertype of α" (lines 624-626, continued on p. 11:13). [E-Sub]'s premises: `Δ' = Δ ∪ {{χ} <: P <: {η}}`, the left side's parameters bound as constants; `σ = [γ/Q]`, `γ ≠ Bottom`, σ within `Q`'s bounds; `Δ' ⊢ α <: σα'`. Existential subtyping `⊑` first reduces the left side (Figure 6, "Existential subtyping"), which changes nothing for a domain without parameters. *Sharpens* § 4: one domain is below another by one substitution for the right side's parameters, found after the left side's are opened as constants. That is the premise row 682 turns on (§ 7.2).
- **[Meet-Excl] and existential reduction (Figure 5; pp. 11:13-14).** `Δ ⊢ (dom(d) ⊓ dom(d')) ⊑ ∃[[]]Bottom`; the reduction "first collects constraints C that make α different from Bottom" (lines 733-736). The worked `ArrayList`/`List` case takes its exclusion from [Anc-Same-Trait] under invariance: "any subtypes of theirs are exclusive unless they are both ArrayList[[S]] for some type S" (p. 11:13, lines 681-683). *Sharpens* § 2: in FGFV two instances of one invariant trait at different arguments exclude, and an object excludes what it does not extend; two unrelated traits never do, since nothing forbids a class extending both. The block's pairs need `Array[\T,I\] ⊓ T'` empty for every number type `T'`, which only `Number`'s closure gives; § 2 stands with "two traits never exclude" read as "two unrelated traits".
- **The static return type at run time (§ 5.1, pp. 11:16-17).** "the static types of method invocation expressions must be available at run time" (lines 820-822); [T-Method] annotates `ε.m(ε'): ρ` (Figure 7); [R-Method] carries `g'` (Figure 8); "A ground type g is a dynamically available type, which is an internal type that does not contain type parameters nor Bottom" (lines 844-846); "all the type parameters are instantiated with ground types at run time" (line 884). *Confirms* § 3's clause for phase 5, and *sharpens* it: by Figure 8's grammar a type holding an opened size is no `g`, and the paper's static types never hold an opened variable, so [R-Method] never meets the case; the completion from the argument's descriptor is the revival's addition, as § 3 says.
- **[Dispatch] and [Solve-Step] (Figures 8 and 10, pp. 11:17-19).** The three steps as § 0 states them (lines 929-936); at the mark `=` the match rules "compute the type bounds that make g ... an equivalent type of α" (p. 11:18, lines 941-943), so at an invariant position the ilk is both bounds; [Solve-Step] takes `g' = u'_i ⊓ ⊓{η'}`, and "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom" (lines 1002-1006). *Confirms* §§ 1 and 3: where the ilk fixes the parameter the declared bound is checked after substitution and never solved; the size opened at a call is the value's own.
- **Lemma 5.2 and its assumption (pp. 11:21-22).** "Assume that an internal type α does not contain Bottom, and if α contains any union type or an intersection type γ, γ does not contain any type parameter" (lines 1098-1100); "The explicitly annotated types in method declarations are external types, which do not contain Bottom, union types, nor intersection types" (lines 1105-1106); unions and intersections are internal types, which checking introduces (p. 11:9, lines 443-446). *Sharpens* § 5: a declared type in FGFV holds no intersection at all, with or without a type parameter inside it; `C[\X\] & X` in a signature is outside the paper's declared types altogether. The confinement's reason is stronger than § 5 put it.
- **[Return-Test] (Figure 5, p. 11:13; p. 11:15).** Premises `Δ ⊢ dom(d) ⊑ dom(d')` and `Δ ⊢ ∀[[κ]](α → ρ) ⊑ ∀[[κ, κ']]((α ⊓ α') → ρ')`; the prose, "[Return-Test] ensures that for any instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists an instance of d1 instantiated with σ1 ∘ σ2 ∘ σ that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (lines 769-771). *Confirms* § 4 (row 690) and § 5.
- **What the paper leaves out (p. 11:3, lines 142-144; p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303).** "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way"; "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, they can be added in an obvious way". *Confirms* § 0. Objects "are like Java final classes that cannot be extended" (p. 11:8), the premise of § 3's "a trait is below no instance of an object".
- **§ 3's phrase "the paper's static argument types are ground".** A static type is an external type `τ` (Figure 2, p. 11:8), which may name a type parameter in scope; "ground" is the run time's word (Figure 8). What § 3 needed holds: a static type is never existential. *Sharpens* a word; the point stands.
- **The items marked "by reading".** Top-level functions as the paper's receiver-free case: the paper is silent, unchanged. § 4's applicable-set argument for row 682: overturned, below.

### 7.2 Row 682 settled

**The pair.** `f(x: NatParamT)` beside `f[\nat n\](x: Nt[\n\])`, with `trait NatParamT comprises { Nt[\n\] } where [\nat n\]` and `value object Nt[\nat n\] extends NatParamT` (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenOverloadChecker.fss`). The domains are `∃∅. NatParamT` and `∃n. Nt[\n\]`.

**In the paper's own calculus the pair is valid, and the generic declaration is strictly more specific.** `∃n. Nt[\n\] ⊑ ∃∅. NatParamT`: open `n` as a constant; `Nt[\n\] <: NatParamT` by its `extends`. `∃∅. NatParamT ⊑ ∃n. Nt[\n\]`: [E-Sub] asks for one `γ` with `NatParamT <: Nt[\γ\]`; no ground size serves, since a trait is below no object instance. So [No-Dup-Not-Less] holds for the plain declaration, [Meet-Less] holds for the generic one, and [Return-Test] holds (`String` on both sides; `Nt[\n\] ⊓ NatParamT` is `Nt[\n\]`). The informal rule says the same: the paper's applicable sets are sets of types, "a generic method declaration d is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α, that is, the domain type of D is a supertype of α" (p. 11:5, lines 246-248), and the type `NatParamT` is in the plain declaration's set and in no instance of the generic one. That is walk's result and the row's first reading ("none of its instances takes a `NatParamT`, so the generic one is more specific"). So two sentences above are overturned as attribution: § 4's "the paper's No Duplicates rule refuses the pair (Theorem 4.1, p. 11:15)" and "the checker's refusal is the paper's verdict", with "In short" point 4, § 5's "Row 682: changes (§ 4)", § 6's item 3 and the fourth bullet "For Pavol". The paper, having no `comprises`, no `where` clause and no sizes, cannot see that every `NatParamT` is an `Nt[\n\]`, and accepts the pair.

**What makes them duplicates is the revival's opening rule, in the paper's form of the test.** The specification: an argument whose type is a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `nat` `where`-clause variable, "passed where that listed type is expected with a nat or int parameter in the variable's place, instantiates that parameter, for that call, with the size of the value itself" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:106-116`, the revival's `\revision{revival-comprises}`). The checker: a trait that opens sizes is below `t` when its listed type, its sizes fresh names, is (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:273-286`), one subtype relation for applicability and for the overloading check alike. That rule reads `NatParamT` as `∃n. Nt[\n\]`. Fed to [E-Sub] it gives `∃∅. NatParamT ⊑ ∃n. Nt[\n\]` with `σ = [n#7/n]`, to the letter; the domains are then each below the other, and the pair is refused by the No Duplicates Rule in the paper's form (Figure 5), in the 2011 paper's ("if d1 ≤ d2 and d2 ≤ d1 then d1 = d2", `Papers/Types/rules.tick:158-161`; "equally specific (i.e., each more specific than the other)", `:184-185`) and in the specification's ("d1 and d2 are not each more specific than the other", `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:548-549`). The applicable sets agree once the rule is granted: of calls, the specification's measure ("applicable to every call to which d1 is applicable", `overloading.tex:539-541`), each declaration applies to every call the other does; of values, every value of the trait is an `Nt[\k\]`. The 2011 paper adds no second route: its `comprises` clause enters exclusion only (`Papers/Types/exc-spec.tick:96`, `fig-exclusion.tick:117-122`), never subtyping, so its calculus too accepts the pair without the opening.

**How far the analogy carries.** Exactly as far as the opening rule. The paper fixes the form of the test and calls it "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets" (p. 11:13, lines 673-675); it leaves one question it cannot answer, whether a closed trait at a `where`-bound size is the existential of its listed type in the overloading check's subtyping. The revival has answered that question: the opening is on record and built (POSITIONS, "Arithmetic in a size ...", fork 3 at way 4a; FACTS, "The compiled checker accepts arithmetic in a size and opens a value of a trait whose comprises clause lists a type at a where-clause size"), and one subtype relation serving applicability and specificity is the consistent reading: a rule under which the generic declaration applies to every `NatParamT` argument makes the two declarations applicable to the same calls, which is what the No Duplicates Rule forbids, and at a static call on a `NatParamT` neither would be the unique most specific declaration, Theorem 4.1's failure. Walk's acceptance is its load check, which tests the nominal direction only (`Nt[\n\] <: NatParamT`; walk "checks part of this at load"), and its run is unambiguous because an ilk `Nt[\3\]` is strictly below `NatParamT`, so the generic declaration's instance is strictly more specific at every call. One caveat, by reading and not probed: by types, the plain declaration keeps a call of its own if the checker ever gives an argument the union of two listed instances, `Nt[\1\] ∪ Nt[\2\]`, which no single instance of the generic declaration takes and the opening does not open (a union is not a trait); the paper's types include such unions (Figure 8), and whether the checker's join of two listed instances is that union or `NatParamT` decides whether the plain declaration has any call at all.

**The verdict.** Settled for the checker: its refusal follows from the revival's own rules under a test whose form the 2019 paper, the 2011 paper and the specification share; the paper supplies the form and not the verdict. The test `XXXNatOpenOverloadChecker` stays as the refusal it pins (a refusal at compile time is written as an `XXX` compile test, `tests-writing.md`). The row keeps its number and gets a pointer to this section, its notes cell being at the template's limit. What remains is the curator's: the status word (`RETIRED`, the checker's refusal being no gap, or a re-class to walk's load check), and whether walk's load check should refuse the pair too, which is a walk row if he wants it.

**Found on the way: a wording defect of the specification.** `overloading.tex:539-541` defines "more specific" strictly ("and not the other way round"); under that definition "d1 and d2 are not each more specific than the other" (`:548-549`) refuses nothing, and an equivalent pair falls instead to the chapter's Meet Rule (`:551-553`: not excluding, neither strictly more specific, no third strictly more specific than both), which is why the row's note names the Meet Rule where the papers name No Duplicates. The 2011 paper's relation is non-strict (`rules.tick:184-185`). The chapter's No Duplicates sentence needs the non-strict relation, or the definition needs "as specific as" beside it. Reported, not repaired: the specification is not among this check's files.

1. FACTS, the arrays' entry on the family's bound (under "The library's arrays and algebra"): the F-bound's standing against [D-Trait], [D-Object] and [Binding-Step], and the block's pairs through `Number`'s closure; its earlier text in `FACTS-history.md`.

        extends { AnyVector, Array1[\T,0,s0\], AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] }

## 6. What it reverses or bends of his positions

- **Bends the letter of "no blanket ring bound that would exclude integer arrays"** (POSITIONS, "The integration review's checks") on `Vector` and `Matrix`: the ring is on the two traits. Keeps its reason: no integer array is excluded, every integer type being a ring at its own type on the built tower, where the review had read the sketch. Keeps its first half, a check per operation's required capability, on the block, and in the reading that each trait's six products all require the ring. If he holds the letter, the only way that keeps it is 6d, which needs `where` clauses first; until then the 23 sites stay.
- **Moves fork 2 before the switch-over** (POSITIONS, "The array design's three questions are open", "after the switch-over"): already moved by his answer to item 15 and PLAN's batch 13 line, which brings forks 3 and 2 to him next; this judgement follows it and does not widen it.
- **Reverses nothing else.** Route A stands; the exclusion rule stands; storage, the model's text, the diagonal's override and answer 7 stand.

## 7. Found on the way

- **A bound list with a closed trait on an overloaded declaration crashes the checker's overloading stage, and its export stage, and refuses a call that passes the parameter on** (section 2.2, section 3): `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.boundsSubstitution`, `:474-477`, the team's "TODO: FIX THIS FOR OPS". No row names it; the library has no such declaration today, so the landed distance does not show it. A row of its own, with the two `XXX` compiled tests of section 5 as its reproducers.
- **The integration review's premise about integers is false on the built tower.** "The flat sketch gives `Integral[I]` `AdditiveGroup[I]`, not `MultiplicativeRing[I]`" (`reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review.md:49`); the library gives `Integral[\I\] extends { StandardTotalOrder[\I\], MultiplicativeRing[\I\], AnyIntegral }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:443`). The POSITIONS entry that took the review's check carries the premise's conclusion ("that would exclude integer arrays") without it.
- **The two factory sites' cause is in the checker, not the library** (section 2.2): `TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:154-167` tests the written `T` with no bound in scope at the first declaration of each overloaded factory pair. No row names it.
- **The team's `Number` was a ring at `Number`.** The team's bound `T extends Number` gave the bodies `RR64` arithmetic, not `T` arithmetic (`75cca6683:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:273-313`), so the bodies were never well typed at `T` under any library; the fork is route A's obligation, as FACTS says, and not a regression.
- **The two-trait static-parameter bound is the revival's form, not the team's.** No such bound is in the team's library; the revival wrote two in route A's rung, neither overloaded nor over a closed trait, and two walk tests pin it (section 2.5). The grammar allows it (`trait-parameters.tex:40-41`).
- **A stage crash reads as progress in the table.** The variant's `#total` fell by 26 where 23 sites cleared and 6 were hidden by crashed stages; only the per-site list and the `#crash` rows show it. A gate that reads the total alone would take a crash for a gain (row 577's rule, by row and line, holds here too).
- **The 09-29 note's `MaxSumReductionPair` line moved**: `:3262` and `:3268` today, `:3179` in the note and `:3247`, `:3253` in `reviews/array-forks-now.md`.

## For Pavol

A *bound* is the rule on a type parameter. `Vector[\T extends Number\]` says the elements are numbers. The team's `Number` carried plus, minus and times itself. Route A, your decision, moved that arithmetic to each number type at its own type, through the library's algebra traits: `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` gives plus and minus, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` those and times. So `Vector`'s body adds two `T`s and the checker finds no rule for it: 25 of the 153 errors.

The library already bounds generic arithmetic by the algebra trait (`SUM`, `PROD`), and writes two traits where one is not enough: `T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }`.

I recommend both:

- `Vector`, `Matrix` and their family: `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`. "Elements are numbers" stays; the ring brings the arithmetic.
- The scalar block, the array-with-number operators: a bound per operator. `+` and `-` get `AdditiveGroup`; `MIN` and `MAX` get `StandardMin` and `StandardMax`.

Every number type is a ring, integers included, so no integer array is excluded. Your check "no blanket ring bound that would exclude integer arrays" keeps its reason, not its letter.

Measured today: 23 of the 25 errors go, 1 hidden one appears, walk's seven array tests print the same. Found: the checker's overloading check (team code, 2012) crashes on a two-trait bound when one trait is closed like `Number`. So the rung has two halves: that checker fix, test first, then the 77 library lines.

No body, model or specification line changes. It leaves 2 errors (a checker slip at two factories) and 10 that need their own list of ways.

Rejected: the ring alone (loses `Number`'s exclusions); a bound per method (needs `where` clauses, unbuilt, and breaks your diagonal's override); arithmetic on `Number` (reverses route A).

Recommendation: the two-trait bound, one batch 13 rung in two halves. Default: the same.
=====
## 6. Decisions and points for the curator

- **A reading of "Sizes".** "A size left unknown after inference is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value": this judgement reads an opened size as bound, not unknown, since inference binds it to the argument's own as it binds a type parameter. If he reads the entry as refusing any size the call's text does not fix, 4a needs his word, and 4c is what remains.
- **A revision of the revival's own sentence.** `traits.tex:238-240`, written 2026-09-28 ("provided that every static variable that occurs in its static arguments is a static parameter of T"), is widened to admit a `where`-clause variable of the declaring trait. It reverses nothing of his: the sentence followed the Types chapter's determination rule, which did not consider `where`-clause variables; the specification's own `where` section allows them.
- **An array fork built before the switch-over.** Item 15's decision today made batch 13 the first array fork's rung; this follows it and bends nothing further.
- **Walk edited for a checker fork.** About ten lines in walk's loader, so that the library's clause loads. It is the walk half of the same rule and belongs in the rung.
- **Not taken:** 4b. Its measurement is named in section 4; it comes to him with the result, after the switch-over, if the result asks.
- **A line owed to INDEX** for this note, which the brief's "commit only that file" leaves to the coordinator.

## 7. What was measured

Nothing. The brief allows one measurement where it decides between two ways and is not on file. None does: 4a against 4b turns on `reflect`'s run-time cost compiled, which no tree can run before the switch-over (row 307); 4a against 4c and 4d turns on his positions; the parser's acceptance of the clause is settled by the grammar (`TraitObject.rats:100-105`, `NoNewlineHeader.rats:152-170`); walk's stop at load is a reading of `BuildEnvironments.java:927-945`, which the rung's first test shows.

## For Pavol

**The question.** A *size* is a number inside a type, the 16 of `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. Some sizes are known only when the program runs. The library turns such a number into a size with `reflect(x)`. Walk accepts it. The compiled checker refuses it at ten library lines, because it does not know that `reflect`'s result, a `NatParam`, is always some `N[\n\]`.

**What the team left.** Jan-Willem Maessen wrote `reflect` in 2007 with the rule as a comment, `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, and "we ought to build it in and document it in the spec".

**The ways.**

- 4a. Uncomment the team's clause. The checker learns: an argument of type `NatParam`, passed where `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` to that value's own size for that call.
- 4b. Also make `reflect` a run-time primitive. It clears nothing more, since item 15 accepts `reflect`'s body; its gain is speed, measurable after the switch-over.
- 4c. Leave such sizes unsized. The library's own `array[\E\](x)` stays refused.
- 4d. No run-time sizes, the batch size fixed at compile time: decision D's D4, which changes the model's api.
- 4e. A `typecase` that binds a size. No spelling exists; it needs `where` constraints first.

**Cost of 4a.** One checker rung of item 15's size: three checker files, two library lines, ten lines in walk, two specification sentences, an Appendix I entry. It clears the ten sites, four hidden in `Array2` and `Array3`, and later the model's three bridges.

**What it bends.** It widens one revival sentence of 28 September. It reads your "Sizes" entry anew: an opened size is bound, not unknown.

**Order.** Beside item 15's rung, in batch 13's gate; its library line not before item 15's part (b).

**Recommendation.** 4a, the team's clause and rule. Default 4a; 4b deferred.

Left: `distribute`'s pairs (row 433), and `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///`, a refused shape unseen only while the checker skips symbolic operators (rows 584, 585). Gated by `tests/LibraryMeetDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-84 **The one library's numbers, orderings, `List` and natives answer their declared types, and its result-only parameters are unbounded, as the team declared them.** `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s nullary comprehension carry an unbounded `T` (P-48), so where `()` is expected their instance is `()`. `MatchFailure` is unchecked. Left: `LexicographicOrder` (row 634's list half), `AnyList`'s readings (row 636) and `QQ`'s power (rows 438, 445). Gated by `tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-order-slips/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5.
- F-85 **The one library's generator, condition, reduction and nested-generator slips are repaired in its own spelling, and three sites of the distance are left there.** They are the identities' numeral fallback (row 436), `embiggen` (row 631) and `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm (row 632). `Condition`'s `cond` calls write their result type as static argument. F-93 holds a generator's size and index (row 629), and F-144 the reductions' `Any` devices (row 628). Gated by `tests/GeneratorDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 8.
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion, and its refused examples are the library's shapes; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. Each refused example stays, marked "Not allowed", beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). The checker does not yet refuse two cases (rows 406, 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the later Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type, and a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between.** A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. A listed bare type variable stays open (row 407). The checker departs in rows 487, 489 and 490. Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2.
- F-146 **The compiled checker accepts arithmetic in a size and opens a value of a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size.** It builds P-55, with array fork 3 at its default. A name or an operation beside a numeral counts as not known to differ, and two different size parameters as different (row 683, contested). The checker opens each listed type's `nat` and `int` `where`-clause sizes as fresh names, and walk reads them as any size. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatArith*` and `NatOpenChecker`.
